title: Hubble launched with a mirror ground wrong by 2 micrometres, and it blurred everything

cover.alt: The Hubble Space Telescope floating above Earth, photographed from Space Shuttle Atlantis during the 2009 servicing mission.

body: Weeks after its launch on 24 April 1990, Hubble’s first images came back blurred. The outer edge of its 2.4 m primary mirror had been polished too flat by about **2.2 micrometres**, because a lens in the test instrument used to check its shape was 1.3 mm out of position. The error was tiny but it spread each star’s light over a radius of more than an arcsecond instead of the 0.1 arcsecond the design demanded. In December 1993 shuttle astronauts installed corrective optics called COSTAR and a new camera, WFPC2, with the correction built into its own mirrors, and the telescope finally saw as sharply as intended.

slides.question: By how many micrometres was the mirror’s edge too flat?
slides.explanation: Just 2.2 micrometres (2,200 nanometres), yet enough to smear starlight over more than an arcsecond instead of the 0.1 arcsecond specified.

slides.heading: The blur: area of a star’s image, flawed versus design
slides.note: Light spread over a radius of more than 1 arcsecond instead of 0.1: about 100 times the area

slides.alt: Two views of the core of galaxy M100: blurred on the left before the 1993 repair, sharp on the right afterwards.
slides.caption: The core of galaxy M100 before (left) and after (right) the December 1993 servicing mission.

slides.heading: Why the test lied
slides.text: The mirror was polished with great precision to the wrong shape. Its curve was checked with a reflective null corrector whose lens had been assembled 1.3 mm out of place, so the instrument reported a perfect mirror while the edge sat 2.2 micrometres too low.

events.text: Launched on the space shuttle Discovery
Shuttle astronauts fit corrective optics and a new camera

slides.question: Why was the mirror ground to the wrong shape?
options: A test lens was 1.3 mm off
slides.explanation: The null corrector used to check the mirror’s curve had a lens out of position by 1.3 mm, so the mirror was polished with great precision to a slightly wrong shape.
